paragraphs.text: Parents today often fill their children’s weeks with lessons, clubs and training sessions. The intention is good, and I do not doubt that many children enjoy these activities. Yet I believe something valuable is being lost.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Unstructured play, in which children decide for themselves what to do, teaches them to solve problems, negotiate with friends and cope with boredom. None of these skills appears on a certificate, which may be why they are so easily overlooked.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Some parents say that organised activities keep children safe and away from screens. That is a fair point, but the choice is not simply between a football club and a tablet. A park or a back garden offers both freedom and fresh air.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: I am not suggesting that clubs should be abandoned. One or two activities a week can give a child real skills and confidence. The problem begins when every evening is booked and a free afternoon is treated as a wasted one.
paragraphs.label: D

items.prompt: The writer doubts that children enjoy organised activities.
The writer thinks unstructured play develops useful skills.
The writer believes schools should set less homework.
The writer dismisses the view that organised activities keep children safe.
The writer believes that one or two activities a week can benefit a child.
